narrative:
The model determined that you have a 68% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is well above the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly forecasts difficulty passing the bar.

Your family income was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction. Coming from an upper-middle income background (the most common bracket among accepted students) slightly improved the outlook, yet it was not nearly enough to offset the academic concerns.

In short, the model concluded that your law-school grades placed you at high risk of failing the bar, and this risk outweighed everything else in your profile.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking tutoring, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program that has a proven track record for students with similar profiles. Once you can demonstrate clearer progress, reapplying with stronger evidence of improvement will significantly raise your chances.
